explanation: Horace Walpole invented serendipity in a 1754 letter, after a tale of three princes of Serendip. William Whewell suggested scientist in 1834, when natural philosopher was the usual term.

claims.text: Horace Walpole coined the word serendipity in a letter of 1754.
William Whewell coined the word scientist in 1834.
Walpole based serendipity on a tale called The Three Princes of Serendip.
Before the word scientist, people who studied nature were usually called natural philosophers.

evidence.restatement: Before scientist, people who studied nature were usually called natural philosophers or men of science.
Horace Walpole coined serendipity in a letter of 28 January 1754 to Horace Mann.

Whewell proposed the word scientist at the British Association's 1833 meeting at Cambridge and it first appeared in print in 1834; accounts split between 1833 for the coinage and 1834 for the first printing.

claimResults.note: The claim 'coined in 1834' conflicts with the common 1833 dating. I could not run a search to settle which date sources favour (WebSearch budget exhausted), so the year as written is uncertain. The answer is unaffected: serendipity (1754) is first on either date.
